# Proposal Standards That Win and Teach

Source: https://lowob.com/research/proposal-standards/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-03 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Buyers now evaluate suppliers with fewer seller interactions, in groups of a dozen or more, so a proposal has to make the case without its author in the room. A proposal standard sets what every proposal must prove and who signs it off. Tagged with its outcome and the buyer's reasons, each proposal also becomes evidence the firm can learn from.

A proposal standard is a short, written rule set that says what every proposal must prove, which sections it must contain, who reviews it and what gets recorded once the buyer decides. It matters because the proposal is now read mostly by people the seller never meets. Forrester's 2024 survey found an average of 13 people involved in a B2B purchase, and Gartner's 2026 survey found two-thirds of buyers preferred a rep-free experience. A proposal that wins makes the case for change, the case for this supplier and the case for acting now, in that order, for readers who were not in the room. A proposal that teaches is tagged with its outcome and the buyer's reasons, so the next one starts from evidence.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most firms have a proposal template. Fewer have a proposal standard. The template fixes the fonts and the order of sections. The standard fixes what each section must prove, what evidence counts and who has to agree before the document leaves the building.

The difference shows up after the decision. A firm with templates has a folder of past proposals and a vague sense of which ones won. A firm with a standard has a record: each proposal tagged with its outcome, the buyer's stated reasons and the decision behind its pricing. This piece covers both halves: the standard that helps a proposal win, and the record that lets each one teach.

## Who actually reads the proposal

The seller writes for the person they met. The proposal is read by everyone else. Forrester's *State of Business Buying 2024*, a survey of more than 16,000 buyers, found an average of 13 people inside the buying organisation involved in a decision, with 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Finance, procurement, IT and the eventual users each read for something different, and most of them will form their view from the document.

Buyers also do more of their evaluation alone. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Its 2025 survey of 632 buyers found that buyers turned to sellers mainly for tasks needing contextual judgment, such as whether a product fits their needs, and that 69% had found mismatches between what a supplier's website said and what its sellers told them. A proposal that contradicts the website, or that cannot be summarised accurately by a buyer's AI assistant, loses ground before anyone reads it closely.

The third fact is indecision. Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's research on about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found that 40–60% of lost deals were lost to indecision, and that calls with high buyer indecision were won about 6% of the time. Forrester reported that 86% of purchases stall. Many proposals are written as if the buyer's only choice is between suppliers. More often the choice is between acting and waiting.

## What a proposal must prove

A useful standard defines a proposal by what it must prove, not by what it must contain. Three cases, in order, cover most B2B decisions.

The case for change: why the buyer should act at all, stated in the buyer's terms and numbers. This is where the metrics and pain gathered in qualification belong (Part 20 compared the frameworks that collect them). Without it, the proposal is a quote.

The case for this supplier: why this firm, against the named alternatives, including doing nothing. Evidence here should be specific and checkable: comparable work, named methods, references the buyer can call. The piece on [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/) covers the standard for this kind of evidence.

The case for acting now: what it costs to wait, what the first step is and how risk is limited. This is the section that answers indecision. A smaller first phase, a clear exit point or a guarantee on a defined outcome all reduce the buyer's fear of getting it wrong.

| Section | What it must prove | Evidence that counts | Who signs it off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Summary (one page) | The whole case, readable without the rest | The buyer's own figures and stated objectives | Account owner |
| The buyer's situation | That the firm understood the problem | Quotes or figures from discovery, confirmed with the buyer | Account owner |
| Proposed approach | That the approach fits this buyer, not buyers in general | Method, phases, named team, comparable work | Delivery lead |
| Evidence | That the firm has done this before | Case studies, references, outcomes with dates | Account owner |
| Commercials | That price and terms are clear and defensible | Price, assumptions, what is excluded, approved discount if any | Finance or deal desk |
| Risk and first step | That acting now is safer than waiting | Phase one scope, exit points, decision date | Account owner and delivery lead |

The summary deserves its own rule. It should stand alone, because it is the page most readers will see and the page an AI assistant will most often be asked to condense. If it cannot be read by the CFO in two minutes and understood, the rest of the document will not rescue it.

> The proposal is read by people the seller never met. Write it for them, not for the meeting.

## Review gates

A standard needs a small number of review points with named owners. Too many and the proposal arrives late; too few and pricing or delivery promises slip through.

| Gate | Question it answers | Owner | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qualification | Should we write this at all? | Sales manager | Before drafting starts |
| Solution | Can we deliver what we are about to promise? | Delivery lead | Before the approach section is final |
| Commercials | Is the price inside policy, and is any exception approved and recorded? | Finance or deal desk | Before pricing is shared |
| Final read | Does the summary stand alone, and does it match what the buyer has seen elsewhere? | Someone outside the deal | Before sending |

The qualification gate saves the most time. Responding to every request for proposal is a common way to lose money in a services firm. A recorded pursue-or-pass decision, with reason and owner, is one of the ten classes in [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/), and it is the cheapest proposal decision to get right.

The commercials gate connects the proposal to discount governance (Part 21). Any discount in the proposal should already carry its reason, its trade and its approver. The final read is the gate firms skip. It needs someone who was not in the meetings, because their confusion is the closest proxy for that of the readers the seller never met.

Forrester's analysts have reported that sellers have access to about 1,400 sales assets on average, and that pricing and implementation options carry more weight late in the buying process. A standard should therefore name the few approved sources for each section, rather than leaving sellers to search a library.

## How each proposal teaches

The second half of the standard happens after the buyer decides. Every proposal should be tagged with four things: the outcome (won, lost, no decision), the buyer's stated reasons, the price offered against the price realised, and the date of the decision.

The buyer's reasons are the hard part, and the seller's own account is not enough. Clozd, a win-loss research vendor, reports that buyer and seller explanations of lost deals align only about 15% of the time in its interview data. The explainer on [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) covers how to get the buyer's view, and [What is a closed-lost reason?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/) covers how to code it.

Once tagged, the proposal library becomes evidence. After two quarters a firm can compare won and lost proposals on things it controls: whether the summary used the buyer's figures, whether a phased first step was offered, how far the price moved from the first draft. Those comparisons are the material for revising the standard. They are also what makes a proposal library useful to an AI assistant later: a model drafting from tagged, outcome-linked proposals is drawing on what worked, not just on what was written.

Illustrative example: adding a first-step section

Decision
:   Make a priced, time-limited first phase a required section in every proposal above a set value.

Reason and owner
:   Two quarters of tagged proposals showed most large losses ending in no decision, and buyer interviews cited the risk of a full commitment. Agreed by the head of sales and the delivery lead; owned by the proposal manager.

What changed
:   Every large proposal now offers a first phase with an exit point. The firm will compare no-decision rates for the following two quarters before deciding whether to extend the rule to smaller proposals.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consulting and implementation firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write for the readers you never meet.** A dozen people may read the proposal; most will not have been in the meeting.
- **Prove three cases in order.** Change, this supplier, and acting now; the third answers indecision.
- **Gate before writing, not only before sending.** The pursue-or-pass decision saves more time than any edit.
- **Tag every proposal with its outcome and the buyer's reasons.** That is what turns a folder of documents into evidence.

Gateway card

### Before you adopt a proposal standard

- A one-page summary rule that the summary must stand alone
- The six standard sections and what each must prove
- Four review gates with named owners and timing
- A recorded pursue-or-pass decision before drafting starts
- Approved sources named for evidence and commercials
- An outcome tag on every proposal: result, buyer's reasons, price offered and realised, decision date

## Next move

Take your last five lost proposals and hand the summary page of each to someone who was never involved. Ask them to say, in one sentence, why the buyer should act now. Where they cannot, that is the section the standard should fix first.
